hints: Look at what happens to the white precipitate when excess sodium hydroxide is added, this tells you if the hydroxide is amphoteric.
Recall that $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ to form a soluble complex, while $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ does not.
For K, think about which silicon compound reacts violently with water to give acidic fumes and a solid, and which one is inert to water.
walkthrough:
**Identify J from the NaOH test**

Both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ give a white precipitate with a few drops of $\text{NaOH(aq)}$. The key is excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2 \text{ (white ppt, insoluble in excess)}$$

**Spot the amphoteric hydroxide**

Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so it redissolves in excess alkali to give a colourless solution. Magnesium hydroxide is basic only, so it stays as a precipitate.

$$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{[Al(OH)}_4\text{]}^- \text{ (dissolves)}$$

**Conclude J is aluminium chloride**

Since the precipitate dissolves, J must contain $\text{Al}^{3+}$. So J is $\text{AlCl}_3$.

**Identify K from the water test**

$\text{SiO}_2$ is a giant covalent oxide and is insoluble and unreactive with water. $\text{SiCl}_4$ is a covalent liquid that hydrolyses vigorously.

$$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2 + 4\text{HCl}$$

**Match observations for K**

The $\text{HCl}$ produced gives misty white fumes and a strongly acidic solution with pH less than 7. The $\text{SiO}_2$ produced appears as a white precipitate. This matches exactly, so K is $\text{SiCl}_4$.

options.A: Correct. J is $\text{AlCl}_3$ because $\text{Al(OH)}_3$ is amphoteric and dissolves in excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$. K is $\text{SiCl}_4$ because it hydrolyses in water to give $\text{SiO}_2$ (white precipitate) and $\text{HCl}$ (misty fumes, pH < 7).
options.B: Incorrect for K. $\text{SiO}_2$ does not react with water, it is insoluble and has no reaction. It cannot produce misty fumes of $\text{HCl}$ or an acidic solution. Students choosing this may have correctly identified J but forgotten that silicon dioxide is inert to water.
options.C: Incorrect for J. $\text{MgCl}_2$ gives $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, a white precipitate that does NOT dissolve in excess $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ because it is not amphoteric. Students choosing this may have remembered both give white precipitates but missed the crucial dissolving in excess test.
options.D: Incorrect for both. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is insoluble in excess alkali, so the precipitate would remain. $\text{SiO}_2$ shows no visible change with water. This row predicts no dissolving and no fumes, opposite to the observations.
